svg.aria-label: Four-frame step sequence showing heap pollution through generic varargs. Frame 1: a batch method takes List of Money varargs batches with no @SafeVarargs annotation; javac warns of possible heap pollution because batches is really a List array at runtime. Frame 2: that array is widened to Object array and javac separately warns about unchecked generic array creation. Frame 3: a List of String is stored into a slot declared List of Money, which array covariance permits with no compiler check. Frame 4: reading that slot back out as Money inserts a checkcast that fails at an unrelated line, producing the real exception ClassCastException: class java.lang.String cannot be cast to class Money, at Leak2.main(Leak2.java:13) — far from where the pollution was written. A closing panel lists the three conditions required for @SafeVarargs to be an honest annotation on a varargs method.
svg.text: HEAP POLLUTION THROUGH GENERIC VARARGS — List<Money>... batches
FRAME 1 — NO @SafeVarargs, AND A List[] AT RUNTIME
static List<Money>[] batch(List<Money>... batches) {
No @SafeVarargs on this signature.
Runtime reality: batches is a List[] — one fresh array per call.
javac -Xlint:varargs
Leak2.java:5: warning: [unchecked] Possible heap
pollution from parameterized vararg type List<Money>
A warning, not an error — compilation still succeeds.
FRAME 2 — THE ARRAY WIDENS TO Object[] AND IS WRITTEN TO
Object[] array = batches;
array[0] = /* Frame 3 */;
List[] widens to Object[] — array covariance permits this,
with zero compiler check on what gets stored into array[0].
javac -Xlint:unchecked
Leak2.java:12: warning: [unchecked] unchecked generic
array creation for varargs parameter of type List<Money>[]
The array's reified type is raw List, not List<Money>.
FRAME 3 — A List<String> IS STORED WHERE List<Money> WAS DECLARED
array[0] = List.of("not money");
A List<String> is written into the slot declared List<Money>.
Legal at compile time: List<String> IS-A List (erased, raw type).
This is the heap pollution — no exception yet.
HEAP STATE AFTER THE WRITE
batches[0] declared: List<Money>
batches[0] actually holds: List<String>
Invisible until something reads that slot as List<Money>.
FRAME 4 — THE ClassCastException FIRES AT AN UNRELATED READ SITE
Money m = result[0].get(0);
get(0) returns "not money" (a String) as Object;
the compiler's inserted checkcast to Money fires right here —
line 13, far from the line 8 write that polluted the array.
The pollution and the failure are in different methods entirely.
REAL EXCEPTION — java Leak2
Exception in thread "main"
java.lang.ClassCastException: class java.lang.String
cannot be cast to class Money (java.lang.String is in
module java.base of loader 'bootstrap'; Money is in
unnamed module of loader 'app')
at Leak2.main(Leak2.java:13)
THE THREE CONDITIONS FOR @SafeVarargs TO BE HONEST
1. The method never stores anything into the varargs array.
2. The method never lets a reference to the varargs array escape to untrusted code.
3. The method is static, final, or private, or is a constructor — it cannot be overridden.
batch(...) above breaks (1) — array[0] = ... — and breaks (2) by returning batches itself.
@SafeVarargs on this method would be a lie; the fix is to stop storing into and returning the array.
A method that only reads its varargs elements (e.g. Arrays.asList-style) can honestly carry the annotation.
